sections.narration:
Welcome. Today we are exploring Return After an Interruption. You are halfway through a point when someone speaks over you. By the time they finish, you feel you have lost your place and your permission to speak.

In this session, we will keep a bookmark for your point, choose whether to return, and use a respectful bridge. I will explain the idea, show a visual example, and invite you to try it in a small experience of your own. You can ask me a question or switch to reading at any point. We will finish by choosing what, if anything, you want to take into a real conversation.

sections.narration: An interruption changes the timing of the exchange; it does not automatically remove your right to finish. First identify whether you still want to complete the point. Then use a short bridge to return. You can say I want to finish that thought, or the point I was making is. You do not need to recreate the exact sentence you were saying.

sections.narration:
You are halfway through a point when someone speaks over you. By the time they finish, you feel you have lost your place and your permission to speak.

People interrupt for different reasons, including enthusiasm, habit, urgency or disregard. You do not have to solve the motive before choosing a response. You can welcome some overlaps and set boundaries around others. Your preference about sentence completion is also legitimate and can be stated directly.

What if I cannot remember my original sentence?

Return to the main meaning rather than the exact sentence. A bookmark such as delivery timing or my main concern gives you a place to begin again. You can say the important point is and continue in new words. If the thought is genuinely gone, you can choose to return later. That is a practical adjustment, not proof that an interruption has taken away your ability to contribute.

sections.narration: For this next attempt, keep one clear purpose. After this prepared interruption, return if you want: That reminds me of something else. Changed, unchanged or uncertain experiences are all information.

exercise.scenario: You are halfway through a point when someone speaks over you. By the time they finish, you feel you have lost your place and your permission to speak.
partnerPrompts: Tell me about a plan you are making.

sections.narration: You are not responsible for making yourself impossible to interrupt. A clear voice and posture are options, while the other person remains responsible for their behaviour. Sometimes a private follow-up is the best route. A changed, unchanged or uncertain experience is information, not a grade. You do not have to report relief for this attempt to count as exploration.

sections.narration: Use a short bookmark before a meeting contribution. If interrupted, decide whether to return now or later. During focused practice, you can deliberately explore this one tool. In an everyday conversation, give most of your attention to the message and the other person. A familiar support can be available if it helps; you do not have to monitor the tool throughout the exchange.
